lines.text: But what if it strips off the metallic form of gold?
It will spit out the beautiful gold, it will despoil it.
What if the form is incorruptible, inseparable, so that it remains gold?
What if it is not gold, if the form of gold is stripped away?
I was expecting a herald who would extol the fame of gold; I experience a robber who takes away the form of gold.
But he induces a new, irreducible one.
New and irreducible do not cohere.
Irreducible was induced before, and extracted, but it cannot be reduced so that it is the same as it was before.
It is neither the same new thing, nor was it induced and extracted before.

But to induce new, intrinsic forms, and therefore faculties from forms, and therefore dispositions to faculties—not of art, not of the craftsman, but of Nature, the architectonic maker, the art of God which is held, is considered a divine work.
In the purest gold, what is impure?
Or how much of it is there, so that it is therefore separated?
But he separates the soul from the body here.
"Death is in the pot": which Nature hates.
Is the soul to be looked at, handled, noted?
Let him send me the body of the gold; I remit the soul to him.
Is the body of gold impure?
But gold is extremely homogeneous to this; whose particles are of the same reason: so either both parts are pure, or it is impure.
Spirits are as impure as bodies: and why not more so?
Some spirits harm by their breath; indeed, they even kill.
We have heard of spiritual poisons, and they are capital; compared to which material ones are little mortal.
In evils, even those are barely harmful, these are most harmful: the force is slower in those; but more violent in these.
If there is any virtue in gold, it is in the body: if there is any virus, it is in the spirit.
Fire does not delete this, but renders it worse, and nearly deleterious: as almost happens in others.
But whether it can be prepared (whether it can be compared by our own effort, or prepared by another's art) is a question called into controversy.
Controversy and question, as they differ: unless this one is through tortures.
The example does nothing, which resolves a suit with a suit.
Indeed, the question precedes, by which it is asked whether it exists, what it is, what it can do, how it can be prepared.
But here is a cart before the horse.
Alas, he will be detected: the mask is stripped away.
If I advise what is to be done, let him confess at last, I would urge, let him confess: let him put down the ridiculous mask.
The one salvation for the defeated is to hope for no salvation.
For he has entangled not only his feet but his head in these shackles: and he imprudently brings not only his fortunes into danger, but also his hunger and faith into crime.
As great as that which the Chemists daily, promiscuously, not only dare but strive to commit, unpunished and immune, and πλανοὶ ἀνυπεύθυνοι.
Why then do I not sing to him that from Horace?
O ship, will new surges carry you back out to sea?
Unless you owe A mockery to the winds, beware.
Are the waves of the Chemists not waves, and indeed triple waves?
But so be it, he says; So be it: let men roar with shouting, the ropes with creaking, The heavy wave with the incursion of waves, the ether with thunder.
Rare swimmers appear in the vast abyss. and so The art fails, and the spirits fall; and as many deaths are seen to rush and break in as there are waves coming.
If the way is smooth, the way is sound; if the voice of the people is the voice of God; if it is endoxa dokounta pasi, what is more true than what is known to the common people?
What is more infallible than what is commonly confessed?
Sometimes the common people see rightly, and sometimes they err.
But they have passed sentence concerning raw gold.
Does he prefer this, or the elixir?

Indeed, if gold is also contained under the name of aes by the most learned lawyer Ulpian, although here it may not be in my copper (perhaps in another's), I shall challenge him with his own copper, and I shall ask him why the earth resists the rust of the earth for gold more than the rust of gold?

Chrysocolla joins gold to gold with copper-smiths' tools: nor does rust of copper offer itself anywhere to burn gold, nor to erode it, nor to pollute it, let alone the earth's: who would resist someone offering no force, bringing no vice?
I. Potable Gold, whether it exists.
Soldiers clash over this, and most believe that it remains uncertain where victory stands.
The Platonists do not agree, nor do the Peripatetic schools.
I. On Potable, drinkable, and portable gold.
But here is the doubt: is it golden, or gilded; is it a lion, or covered in a lion's skin; is it a mystes, or one carrying mysteries?
Behold a face shining from afar, behold the splendid beginnings that Pindar persuades.
Why does Euphormio sing the triumph of Gold?
The doors themselves rattle with gold.
Golden-mouthed, and a beautiful head, whether golden, or brazen, or wooden, or earthen, when gold speaks, who is not enticed to listen?
Who, gaping, does not embrace it?
Although it is a head, yet it is not this --a body without a heart.
Let the Lydian stone test the gold: the gold will test the man.
A proverb among the French: It is gold, which is worth gold.
But I fear that in a golden scabbard a leaden sword may be enclosed.
But that takes away not the form and mixture, but the continuity: therefore it is still reducible.
The internal form does not perish.
Sophists philosophize for Cicero; but either for the sake of ostentation, or for gain: thus Chemists.
If, therefore, all causes of the corruption of metals agree, it is necessary that bodies be corrupted most of all.

Gold, therefore, is a most precious stone, lacking spots, tempered also; neither fire, nor water, nor earth can corrupt the universal ferment, rectifying all things through a tempered composition, which is of a yellow, or true citrine color.
The gold of the wise, cooked and well-digested, makes an elixir from fiery water.
For the gold of the wise is heavier than lead, which is a ferment of elixir in tempered composition; and on the contrary, it is distempered in a distempered composition.
Also Maria said of it: Take the body of the magnesia which has been whitened and made similar to leaves, because it is that which puts poverty to flight, since it has no other medicine after God.

Then the author is brought in against the vain workers of this art, who have neither root nor preparation in the least, saying: Every preparation is good for that thing, except this hidden preparation of the Philosophorum: but they themselves composed the prohibition of it in their act, because they always prepare, and are never prosperous.
And so that their error may be more confirmed, and that they do not despair of that which they seek, they cannot [attain it], but they hope to find it.

And concerning the composition of false books, Senior says: For he composed his book, thinking that he understood that hidden mystical thing, and he himself neither knows nor understands one letter of those things which he composed in his book, removed from the books of the Philosophorum.
And if it is asked of him, he answers from them through similarity, and if they are proven to him, he defends himself through cavils and vain similarities.

And note that not everything should be put into the preparation at once, as the experts do—that is, one part should be tested so that no error occurs in the whole—or two in which your vessels may hang.
It is more tolerable to prolong under moderation than to sin irrecoverably under excess.
The experts, however, poured water over it so that it exceeded by three fingers, according to what seemed good to them.

To bring about its perfection, there is one that is read more truly: 21, another 61 days it has, days for dissolution, for the first leading 13 days, for the completion 40 days, according to what nature and fire will teach you.
Follow its nature according to the signs and keys handed down, and they will not permit you to err.

Let the humid and white stone, well-fermented, be taken, and let it be washed with one third of nine, and let it putrefy little by little and part by part, until it is whitened in 150 days—that is, 21 days of one name—and this is according to Senior.
He says that the first luminous work is to wash, to whiten, and to putrefy for 150 days, and this is the whitening of the whole and the flight of shadows from it.
And perhaps whiteness will appear in 70 days, that is, 10 weeks.
Do not therefore be deceived by the plurality of names, but hold it as certain that each one is what it is, to which nothing alien is added.
Therefore, investigate its companion, that is, brass, and add nothing else to it, and let men multiply names; if they were not multiplied, children would mock our wisdom.
Such a one who does this seeks boasting.

For he composed his book thinking that he understood that occult mystical thing, and he himself does not know, nor does he understand one letter of those things which he composed in his book, and if anything is asked of him from them, he responds through falsehood.
And if he is proven wrong, he defends himself through cavil and vain similitudes.
It is open to studious, wise, and intelligent investigators, but concealed to the less intelligent.
Because as Rafis says in the Book of Lights: It never becomes black at the end, and if anything black proceeds, the medicine is imperfect.

And Senior says: If blackness remains in it after its rubification, you have sinned in its preparation, and you have corrupted whatever you have worked, and you will die from the pain of sin and poverty, because these are incomparable riches.

The three higher ones, however, are an image of divine spirituality, in which is carried water, which they call gold, and they name this divine water of the nature of all moisture, from vinegars, urines, and milks, fats, bloods, and sperms.

Similarly, they name this water the vivifying Cloud, the lower world, and by all these things they understand the Aqua foliata, which is the gold of the Philosophers, which the master Hermes called the Egg, having many names.
And the third is the earth of gold, which is the solar tincture and the earth itself after the blackening.
The second, once whitened, is called the gold of the Philosophers.

And the water is their gold, because it is the mother of gold, because it generates gold, according to Senior: And those three earths are one nature of one sphere, and of one kind: and it is to be understood similarly regarding the three saltings, and salted things, that is, the imbibitions with three thirds of nine parts.
To this question it must be said that the water is coagulated with the tincture, and I have seen [this] through experience.
Indeed, all the sages said, Do not cause anything alien to enter upon it, for it corrupts it.
But if it enters, it will destroy it, and this will never be concluded with our stones and our bodies.
There are six of them, namely: Gold, Silver, Lead, Tin, Brass or Copper, and Iron.
We say, therefore, that a metal is a fusible mineral body, extendable under the hammer in every dimension.
A metal is, moreover, of dense substance and very strong composition.
Through this, therefore, we find by truthful discovery a marvelous genus of two secrets.
The first is the triple cause of the corruption of each of the metals by fire.

The first of these causes is the inclusion of burning sulfurousness in the depth of their substance, which, through its inflammation, diminishes the whole substance of the bodies and destroys it into smoke by ultimate consumption, however much argentum vivum of good melting might exist in them.
The second cause is the multiplication of the exterior flame upon them, which penetrates them and resolves them with itself into smoke, regardless of their degree of fixation.
The third cause is the rarefaction of the bodies themselves through calcination.
If, therefore, all the causes of corruption coincide, it is necessary that the bodies be corrupted to the greatest degree.
Similarly, likewise, the examination of this ash-bed can be prepared in an earthen crucible, and blown around it; and similarly upon its face, so that it may be blown around what is to be examined.
These things having been sufficiently narrated, let us pass to the examination by cement, with its causes and its manifest and known experiences.

We have said, therefore, that certain bodies are burned more, and others less, by the mode of calcination through fire: as those which contain a greater quantity of combustible sulfur; and those which contain less, burn less.
Since, therefore, the Sun is of a lesser quantity of sulfur among other bodies, it is for that reason the least burned among all mineral bodies through the inflammation of fire.
The Moon, however, after the Sun, participates the least in the quantity of sulfur among all remaining bodies; yet more than the Sun.
For this reason, some of the Philosophorum thought that the art could not be reached through this.

But we ourselves, in our own time, investigating this science, have arrived at the truth: that likewise, by no manner of preparation of our ingenuity, could we illuminate the bodies with the complement of their bright splendor without it happening that they were entirely corrupted, tainted, and rather, thoroughly blackened.
For which reason, we too were brought into a stupor, and for a long space of time, we hid under the shade of despair.

Returning, therefore, to our heart, tormenting ourselves with the afflictions of immense meditation of thoughts, we looked back from the perfection of the bodies the pores diminished, existing as foul in the depth of their nature: and nothing bright is found in them, since it is not in them according to nature.
That which has held that clear and clean substance is manifested through its resplendent and radiating gleam: revealing itself not only by day, but also by night, and it needs no other proof.
That it possesses a fixed nature without burning sulfur is clear through every operation of it with fire.
For it is neither diminished nor inflamed.

Therefore, the wise artifex should study our volumes, collecting our true intent which has been dispersed; which we have proposed in various places, lest it be published to the wicked or the ignorant.
He should test the collected [knowledge] until, by studying and experimenting with the persistence of an ingenious labor, he arrives at the complete cognition.
Therefore, the artifex should apply himself, and he will find it.
For we consider this science to treat of perfect and imperfect bodies.
It also gives full knowledge of perfecting and of the corruption of matter and form.
EVIDENT AND MANIFEST PROOF OF THE CHEMICAL ART.
Taken from the Antiquities of Petrus Apianus.
Some years ago at Padua, a wonderful argument for the Alchemical art was discovered.

Inside this urn, another smaller one was found; when it was opened, two flasks were discovered, elaborately crafted; one made of silver, the other of gold, filled with a very pure liquid, by which a lamp still burning is believed to have been preserved for very many centuries.

On the little urns, these verses were inscribed: > Go away from here, worst of thieves, > What do you want with your prying eyes? > Go away from here with your Mercury wearing a hat and carrying a caduceus; > The Greatest makes this gift sacred to the greatest Pluto.

Through this, therefore, you will be able to elicit a great secret: Since bodies with a greater quantity of argentum vivum are found to be of the greatest perfection; therefore, the more the quantity of argentum vivum in bodies that are diminished from perfection, the more they must necessarily approximate to perfection.
For which reason, therefore, from the things already said, it is evident that Jupiter most approximates to the perfect; since it participates in the perfection of argentum vivum more.
Saturn, in truth, less: Venus still less: Mars, in truth, least of all, as far as it depends upon the causes of perfection.

Otherwise, however, with a medicine that perfects, and supplies the defect, and attenuates to the depth of the body, and palliates and tempers their darkness and foulness, and brings forth splendor, it happens that imperfect bodies behave themselves.
From these, therefore, it has been discovered by the truthful investigation of labor that different medicines are found for different metals, along with their preparation.

Furthermore, others argue based on what we see through experience, for this science has reached the ears of the prudent for more than a thousand years, and if it were possible and true, it would have been discovered a thousand times over by now.
Similarly, since the philosophers have not dared to hand it down in their volumes, nor can we find any manifest truth in them, it is sufficiently probable that this science does not exist.

Likewise, many princes of this world, possessing infinite treasure and an abundance of philosophers, desire to find this art; yet they have not been able to reach the fruit of this most precious art, which is surely a sufficient argument that this art is frivolous and a mere fabrication.
SECOND BOOK On the knowledge of the principles of the bodies.
IT is not possible to know this transmutation of bodies and of argentum vivum itself unless a true knowledge of their nature, according to their roots, comes to the mind of the artist.

Therefore, we shall first identify the principles of the bodies according to their roots and their essences; namely, what they are according to all the causes of their differences, and what good or evil they contain within themselves.
THEREFORE, in the first place, we affirm the nature of the spirits, which are the principles of the bodies themselves: these are, namely, sulphur, arsenic, and argentum vivum.
Since, therefore, in a medicine more closely related to the truth, in no way is it possible to find this art, then it is found even less in those more remote; therefore, it is found nowhere.
Our answer, however, is this: because they do not know all that is knowable concerning this matter, therefore the work is not found therein.
They therefore posit the flaw of the conclusion because of the insufficiency of their own work.
Therefore, among all imperfecta corpora, Jupiter exists as the most splendid, most lucid, and of greater perfection.
After it, however, Venus is chosen for a more perfect mutation, being of difficult handling, but of shorter labor than Jupiter.
Saturn, however, after Venus, possesses a perfection in transmutation diminished from hers: for it is of easy handling, but exists as the longest labor.
Mars, however, is found among other imperfect bodies to have the least perfection in transmutation, being of the most difficult handling of all and found to be of the longest labor.
It is appropriate, therefore, now only to narrate the impediments supervening from the outside, from accidents by which this glorious work is hindered.

For we see some who are ingenious and astute, not ignorant of the works of nature, and who follow the principles in this work—insofar as it was possible—and in all its works where there is investigation and phantasia, in all things that are regulated by the actions of nature within the lunar circle.
Yet, these people, oppressed by the utmost poverty and the need for all expenses, are forced to postpone this most excellent masterwork.
There are others who are curious, held back by the vanities, cares, and spectacles of this world, from which this science of ours retreats.
It is now therefore evident from what has been said what the impeding factors are in this art that hold one back, lest anyone attain its end.
For with that, you will find it, and without it, you will not.
But even if we have veiled this, let not the son of doctrine wonder.

For we have not veiled it from him, but we have handed it down to the evil and wicked in such language as must necessarily elude the foolish, while the prudent are enticed by the same to the search for its discovery.
Therefore, sons of doctrine, search for this most excellent gift of God kept for you alone.
Foolish sons of wickedness and malevolent and immense depravity, flee from this science, since it is hostile and adverse to you, and it will set you in the misery of poverty.
Therefore, the medicine of the second order is that which completes the imperfect [body] joined by a single difference of perfection.
And this is what makes them opine that its construction is impossible, because they are ignorant of artificial destruction by the course of nature.
They have perhaps proven that it is of strong composition, but they have not proven of what strength of composition it consists.

spine.title: The Assay: A Trial Without Verdict
spine.logline: In a court that reads evidence for three acts and never rules, an alchemist is tried for promising an incorruptible metal, while the ledger of what the promise cost is entered piece by piece into the record.

dramatisPersonae.name: The Bench
dramatisPersonae.note: The presiding magistrate, who hears everything and pronounces nothing.

dramatisPersonae.name: The Examiner
dramatisPersonae.note: Prosecutor for the crown of physicians; speaks from Matthew Gwinne, 'Gold Not Gold' (1613).

dramatisPersonae.name: The Artifex
dramatisPersonae.note: The accused adept, who conducts his own defence; speaks from Geber, 'Three Books on Alchemy' (1598).

dramatisPersonae.name: The Deposition
dramatisPersonae.note: An absent Eastern witness whose written testimony the court has read aloud; from Ibn-Umail, 'Tabula chymica' (1605).

dramatisPersonae.name: Clerk Vespucci
dramatisPersonae.note: Clerk of the court, who reads exhibits into the record and numbers them.

dramatisPersonae.name: Master Orsolo
dramatisPersonae.note: Sworn assayer to the mint, who handles the exhibits and refuses to say what they are.

dramatisPersonae.name: Bianca Trevisan
dramatisPersonae.note: A widow and creditor, who furnished the coal, the crucibles and the years.

dramatisPersonae.name: The Boy Anselm
dramatisPersonae.note: The Artifex's surviving apprentice, who blew the bellows and lost his sight to the furnace.

beats.summary: The court convenes at dawn. Clerk Vespucci reads the heading of the cause and the state of the dispute; the Bench takes his seat, orders the doors shut, and instructs that nothing be decided until all is read.

Exhibit One, a small stoppered phial, is passed from the Clerk to Master Orsolo and then to the Examiner, who turns it in the light and presses the assayer to distinguish surface from substance. Orsolo declines to swear either way and sets the phial down.

The prosecution enters the objections of the world, taken out of the accused's own printed volume, and the Examiner then turns on the crowd in the gallery, testing how far common opinion may be trusted as a judge of anything.

The defence produces its only physical proof: a nested funerary urn dug up at Padua, with its lamp and its two flasks. Clerk Vespucci reads the provenance and then the inscription cut on the vessels; the Bench orders the urn kept under seal.

acts.title: Act II — The Reading of the Evidence

beats.summary: The absent witness's deposition is read into the record on the question of incorruption. The Examiner interrupts to ask why the earth spares one metal and eats the rest, and the Artifex answers with the tests he himself applies with fire.

Cross-examination. The Examiner demands that the accused point, in the court, to the part of the metal he claims to divide, and offers a bargain across the table which the Artifex will not take; Master Orsolo is recalled and again says nothing.

Exhibit Four: the seized laboratory register. The Clerk reads its measures, waters and counted days aloud in a flat voice while the Boy Anselm, standing at the bar, silently mouths the numbers he once kept by heart.

The Examiner charges that the books are deliberately unreadable. The Artifex admits the veil and defends it; the deposition is read again to show the trade's own contempt for its counterfeiters, and the Bench allows both to stand unreconciled.

The last matter of proof: whether a new form can be laid on a body and never taken off again. The Examiner presses until the words of the claim collide with one another, and marks the contradiction in the margin of the transcript.

Evidence of destruction. Master Orsolo lays out the burnt residues from the seized furnace, and the Artifex, questioned on his own doctrine, itemises how fire undoes a body; the Examiner adds what fire does to what is left.

The accused is invited to speak in his own person and describes the years between the failure and the recovery of nerve, and the two kinds of men who never finish the work at all. The Boy Anselm is led out during this.

Bianca Trevisan is sworn and lays her tallies on the bench: coal, coin, the roof of a house, a husband's health. The Clerk reads back, at her request, the two passages in the seized books that name the wages of the work.

The Examiner rises for the summing-up, strips the exhibit's paper wrapping from the phial, and urges a confession; he ends with a sailor's warning sung out over the heads of the court while the gallery grows loud.

The Bench takes the phial, holds it, and puts it back down. He notes that the questions were asked in the wrong order and adjourns the cause without day; the Artifex, being released to the corridor, addresses the students waiting there, and the Clerk closes the book with the record unsigned.

Three days. I have listened to a controversy that was never a question.

THE BENCH
But whether it can be prepared (whether it can be compared by our own effort, or prepared by another's art) is a question called into controversy. [[src:b1p209l21]]

THE BENCH
Controversy and question, as they differ: unless this one is through tortures. [[src:b1p209l22]]

THE EXAMINER
My lord, no tortures were used.

THE BENCH
No. Only the order of asking.

THE BENCH
Indeed, the question precedes, by which it is asked whether it exists, what it is, what it can do, how it can be prepared. [[src:b1p209l24]]

THE BENCH
But here is a cart before the horse. [[src:b1p209l25]]

CLERK VESPUCCI
How is the cause to be entered?

THE BENCH
Adjourned. Without day. The exhibits to remain in the dishes, the phial to remain unopened, the accused to be released to the corridor.

CLERK VESPUCCI
And the verdict, my lord?

THE BENCH
Write the word adjourned twice, so that nobody can add to it.

THE BENCH rises and goes. The gallery empties past the table. THE ARTIFEX walks out into the corridor, where students are waiting, and THE BOY ANSELM sits on a bench with his bandaged eyes turned up.

A STUDENT
Master, they have not condemned you. What do we do?

THE ARTIFEX
Therefore, the wise artifex should study our volumes, collecting our true intent which has been dispersed; which we have proposed in various places, lest it be published to the wicked or the ignorant. [[src:b3p322l0]]

THE ARTIFEX
He should test the collected [knowledge] until, by studying and experimenting with the persistence of an ingenious labor, he arrives at the complete cognition. [[src:b3p322l1]]

THE ARTIFEX
Therefore, the artifex should apply himself, and he will find it. [[src:b3p322l2]]

BIANCA TREVISAN stands in the doorway with her tallies under her arm and listens.

THE ARTIFEX
Therefore, sons of doctrine, search for this most excellent gift of God kept for you alone. [[src:b3p269l5]]

A STUDENT
And without the gift?

THE ARTIFEX
For with that, you will find it, and without it, you will not. [[src:b3p269l0]]

The students go with him. BIANCA TREVISAN takes the boy's arm and leads him the other way.

In the emptied hall, CLERK VESPUCCI trims his pen, writes two words, and looks at the space left for signatures. He closes the book on the dry ink and carries it out. The nine dishes and the phial stay on the table.

END OF ACT III

spine.title: The Assay
spine.logline: In one locked laboratory over one night, a sceptical physician and an adept of the furnace put each other's claims to the fire, with a dying apprentice and an impatient creditor as the only witnesses.

dramatisPersonae.name: Matthew Gwinne
dramatisPersonae.note: Physician and disputant, speaking from his 'Gold Not Gold' (1613); he denies the art.

dramatisPersonae.name: The Adept
dramatisPersonae.note: Master of the furnace, speaking from Geber's 'Three Books on Alchemy' (1598); he affirms the art.

dramatisPersonae.name: Senior
dramatisPersonae.note: An old translator-copyist attending the furnace, speaking from Ibn-Umail's 'Tabula chymica' (1605).

dramatisPersonae.name: Perrin
dramatisPersonae.note: The Adept's apprentice, mercury-poisoned, mute for most of the night.

dramatisPersonae.name: Madame Vaux
dramatisPersonae.note: The creditor who owns the house and has come for her money by dawn.

beats.summary: Midnight. Madame Vaux locks the door of the laboratory and states her terms: nobody leaves until the two men settle whether the work is real. Gwinne opens by naming the question at issue and reporting that the learned world is deadlocked over it.
The Adept lights the furnace and answers with the framework of his science, laying out what a metal is and what the principles behind bodies are, while Perrin lays out the vessels.

Gwinne presses the mask-question: is the thing before them the substance or only its likeness, and warns what the shining outside of the vessel may conceal. Madame Vaux, hearing only the word 'gold', is drawn in.

Senior, who has copied out these books for forty years, offers the tradition's own definition of the incorruptible metal, and describes the earths through which the work is said to pass. The Adept nods; Gwinne writes it down as evidence against him.

Gwinne rehearses the standard arguments of the deniers — the centuries of failure, the silence of the philosophers, the ruined princes — and the Adept answers that the fault lies in the workmen, not the conclusion.

The dispute narrows to the separation of soul from body in the purest metal. Gwinne demands to know what impurity there could possibly be, and refuses to accept a distinction he cannot see or handle; he offers a bargain about which half he will keep.

Perrin coughs blood into a cloth. Gwinne, examining him, turns the argument to poison: the spirits raised in this room are the killing part, and fire only makes them worse. Senior and the Adept keep working through it.

The Adept counters with the doctrine of corruption and its causes, and with the ranking of the imperfect metals by how far each stands from perfection — his claim being that the defect is measurable, therefore remediable.
Madame Vaux asks the only question she cares about: whether it can in fact be prepared. Gwinne mocks the order of the inquiry itself, saying the whole enterprise has been argued backwards.

acts.title: Act III — The Fire and the Reckoning

beats.summary: Senior takes over the furnace and recites the timetable of the operation aloud — the parts, the washing, the counted days — while Perrin is carried to a bench. The recital is long enough that Madame Vaux begins to understand how much of her money it consumes.

The Adept confesses the low point of his own career: the years when nothing he prepared came out bright, and he hid from the work. He then insists he came out the other side, and charges Senior and Perrin to keep at it.

The vessel is opened. Gwinne examines what is in it and declares that the operation has taken the form away rather than conferred one; he presses the contradiction in claiming a new form that cannot be reduced.

Gwinne turns from argument to advice, urging the Adept to lay down the pretence before it destroys him, and warns him with the image of a ship putting back out to sea. The Adept answers that he accepts the storm.

Dawn. Perrin dies. Madame Vaux unlocks the door and takes the equipment in lieu of payment. Senior, alone, reads out the epitaph on an old buried lamp; the Adept refuses to concede and states what he takes the science to be about, leaving the dispute unresolved.

# ACT 1 — Act I — The Question Posed

ACT I — THE QUESTION POSED

INT. LABORATORY BENEATH THE HOUSE OF MADAME VAUX — MIDNIGHT

*A low vaulted room. A cold furnace. Shelves of glass. PERRIN, thin, grey at the mouth, sits on a stool with his hands in his lap. SENIOR bends over a book with a cut pen. MATTHEW GWINNE stands in his travelling cloak. THE ADEPT waits by the furnace. MADAME VAUX turns the key in the door and puts it down the front of her dress.*

MADAME VAUX
That is the only key. There is no other.

GWINNE
Open it.

MADAME VAUX
At dawn. Not before. This house is mine, the furnace is mine, the coal is mine, and the debt is his. I have paid four years for smoke. Tonight the two of you will settle whether there is anything under the smoke, and I will hear it settled.

THE ADEPT
And if we do not settle it?

MADAME VAUX
Then you will all be here tomorrow night as well.

*She sits. GWINNE takes out a small notebook and opens it flat on the bench.*

GWINNE
Then let the question be stated plainly, and stated first, so that we do not argue two different things until morning. This is the article.

GWINNE
I. Potable Gold, whether it exists. [[src:b1p22l1]]

MADAME VAUX
That is the whole of it?

GWINNE
That is the whole of it. And I will tell you at once that I bring you no verdict, because there is none to bring.

GWINNE
Soldiers clash over this, and most believe that it remains uncertain where victory stands. [[src:b1p22l3]]

MADAME VAUX
Who clashes?

GWINNE
Everyone who has ever held a book. The schools are not merely divided, madame; they are divided upon their own foundations.

GWINNE
The Platonists do not agree, nor do the Peripatetic schools. [[src:b1p22l4]]

THE ADEPT
And you would have me answer a question the schools cannot even hold still.

GWINNE
I would have you answer the one I have written at the head of the page. Here it stands.

GWINNE
I. On Potable, drinkable, and portable gold. [[src:b1p22l6]]

*THE ADEPT takes a coal from the covered pan and sets it into the furnace. He works the bellows twice. PERRIN rises without being told and begins setting outthe vessels along the bench, slowly, in order.*

THE ADEPT
You write your question at the head of a page. Good. I will write mine at the head of the work, and mine comes first, because without it your gold and my gold are only words. Perrin. The flasks.

THE ADEPT
SECOND BOOK On the knowledge of the principles of the bodies. [[src:b3p176l0]]

MADAME VAUX
Bodies. What bodies. I see glass and a sick boy.

THE ADEPT
The metals, madame. That is what we call them. And nothing can be done to them by any hand until the hand knows what they are.

THE ADEPT
IT is not possible to know this transmutation of bodies and of argentum vivum itself unless a true knowledge of their nature, according to their roots, comes to the mind of the artist. [[src:b3p176l2]]

GWINNE
Then begin at the root, since you name it.

THE ADEPT
Therefore, we shall first identify the principles of the bodies according to their roots and their essences; namely, what they are according to all the causes of their differences, and what good or evil they contain within themselves. [[src:b3p176l3]]

THE ADEPT
THEREFORE, in the first place, we affirm the nature of the spirits, which are the principles of the bodies themselves: these are, namely, sulphur, arsenic, and argentum vivum. [[src:b3p176l7]]

*PERRIN sets down the last vessel and touches, one by one, six small ingots laid in a row.*

THE ADEPT
And these are the bodies themselves. Count them.

THE ADEPT
There are six of them, namely: Gold, Silver, Lead, Tin, Brass or Copper, and Iron. [[src:b3p86l6]]

GWINNE
And what, in your school, makes a thing one of the six and not merely a stone that shines?

THE ADEPT
We say, therefore, that a metal is a fusible mineral body, extendable under the hammer in every dimension. [[src:b3p86l7]]

THE ADEPT
A metal is, moreover, of dense substance and very strong composition. [[src:b3p86l8]]

GWINNE
Dense, strong, fusible, hammered thin. Good. Every word of that I can grant you. It is the next word where we part.

*GWINNE steps to the bench and lifts one of the small vessels to the lamp. It gleams.*

GWINNE
Here is my doubt, and it is older than either of us.

GWINNE
But here is the doubt: is it golden, or gilded; is it a lion, or covered in a lion's skin; is it a mystes, or one carrying mysteries? [[src:b1p22l8]]

GWINNE
Behold a face shining from afar, behold the splendid beginnings that Pindar persuades. [[src:b1p22l9]]

MADAME VAUX
Say that again in my language.

GWINNE
A thing may shine like the thing it is not. That is all. The whole art may be a skin.

GWINNE
Golden-mouthed, and a beautiful head, whether golden, or brazen, or wooden, or earthen, when gold speaks, who is not enticed to listen? [[src:b1p22l13]]

MADAME VAUX
*(leaning in)* You said gold.

GWINNE
I said the word, madame. That was my point. The word alone bends the ear before the assay is ever made.

GWINNE
Who, gaping, does not embrace it? [[src:b1p22l15]]

MADAME VAUX
I have been listening four years to that word.

GWINNE
Then you above all should fear it. Because a bright surface is exactly what conceals the base thing under it.

GWINNE
But I fear that in a golden scabbard a leaden sword may be enclosed. [[src:b1p22l19]]

THE ADEPT
Then test it. I do not fear the stone.

GWINNE
Let the Lydian stone test the gold: the gold will test the man. [[src:b1p22l17]]

*SENIOR sets down his pen. He speaks slowly, like a man reading a thing he has copied a hundred times.*

SENIOR
Before you touch it to any stone, know what the books themselves say it is. I have written these words out for forty years. I did not invent one of them.

SENIOR
Gold, therefore, is a most precious stone, lacking spots, tempered also; neither fire, nor water, nor earth can corrupt the universal ferment, rectifying all things through a tempered composition, which is of a yellow, or true citrine color. [[src:b2p137l2]]

MADAME VAUX
Incorruptible.

SENIOR
So they wrote. And they wrote also the road by which the thing is said to come. It passes through earths. Hear them named.

SENIOR
And the third is the earth of gold, which is the solar tincture and the earth itself after the blackening. [[src:b2p189l4]]

SENIOR
The second, once whitened, is called the gold of the Philosophers. [[src:b2p189l5]]

SENIOR
And the water is their gold, because it is the mother of gold, because it generates gold, according to Senior: And those three earths are one nature of one sphere, and of one kind: and it is to be understood similarly regarding the three saltings, and salted things, that is, the imbibitions with three thirds of nine parts. [[src:b2p189l6]]

SENIOR
Similarly, they name this water the vivifying Cloud, the lower world, and by all these things they understand the Aqua foliata, which is the gold of the Philosophers, which the master Hermes called the Egg, having many names. [[src:b2p24l5]]

*THE ADEPT bows his head slightly, as at something correct. GWINNE writes rapidly.*

MADAME VAUX
You nod at that. You, physician, you write it down. You cannot both be pleased.

GWINNE
He is pleased because it is his scripture. I write it down because it is my evidence. The same words, madame. We are only waiting for the fire to say which of us was reading them right.

*THE ADEPT works the bellows. The furnace takes light. PERRIN watches the flame with his grey mouth open, saying nothing.*

# ACT 2 — Act II — The Cross-Examination

ACT II — THE CROSS-EXAMINATION

INT. THE LABORATORY — NIGHT

The furnace breathes. Senior bends over a copied page, his lips moving without sound. Perrin crouches near the coals, a cloth pressed to his mouth. Madame Vaux stands by the barred door, a ledger under her arm. Gwinne circles the bench where the Adept works.

GWINNE
You want my objections. Very well. Take the oldest of them first.

GWINNE
Furthermore, others argue based on what we see through experience, for this science has reached the ears of the prudent for more than a thousand years, and if it were possible and true, it would have been discovered a thousand times over by now. [[src:b3p38l0]]

GWINNE
Similarly, since the philosophers have not dared to hand it down in their volumes, nor can we find any manifest truth in them, it is sufficiently probable that this science does not exist. [[src:b3p38l1]]

GWINNE
Likewise, many princes of this world, possessing infinite treasure and an abundance of philosophers, desire to find this art; yet they have not been able to reach the fruit of this most precious art, which is surely a sufficient argument that this art is frivolous and a mere fabrication. [[src:b3p38l2]]

The Adept does not look up from his crucible.

GWINNE
And if it fails in the noblest matter, it fails in all.

GWINNE
Since, therefore, in a medicine more closely related to the truth, in no way is it possible to find this art, then it is found even less in those more remote; therefore, it is found nowhere. [[src:b3p65l0]]

THE ADEPT
You blame the road because the traveller was lame.

THE ADEPT
Our answer, however, is this: because they do not know all that is knowable concerning this matter, therefore the work is not found therein. [[src:b3p65l1]]

THE ADEPT
They therefore posit the flaw of the conclusion because of the insufficiency of their own work. [[src:b3p65l2]]

GWINNE
Say plainly what you mean.

THE ADEPT
And this is what makes them opine that its construction is impossible, because they are ignorant of artificial destruction by the course of nature. [[src:b3p54l0]]

THE ADEPT
They have perhaps proven that it is of strong composition, but they have not proven of what strength of composition it consists. [[src:b3p54l1]]

Gwinne sets both hands on the bench.

GWINNE
Then let us narrow it. You promise gold made purer than gold. Show me the flaw you intend to burn away.

GWINNE
In the purest gold, what is impure? [[src:b1p150l3]]

GWINNE
Or how much of it is there, so that it is therefore separated? [[src:b1p150l4]]

THE ADEPT
The soul is drawn out from the body. That is the whole art.

GWINNE
But he separates the soul from the body here. [[src:b1p150l5]]

GWINNE
Is the soul to be looked at, handled, noted? [[src:b1p150l7]]

GWINNE
Let him send me the body of the gold; I remit the soul to him. [[src:b1p150l8]]

MADAME VAUX
You would keep the metal and give him the vapour?

GWINNE
Gladly. Now answer me.

GWINNE
Is the body of gold impure? [[src:b1p150l9]]

GWINNE
But gold is extremely homogeneous to this; whose particles are of the same reason: so either both parts are pure, or it is impure. [[src:b1p150l12]]

THE ADEPT
There is virtue in it you have never weighed.

GWINNE
If there is any virtue in gold, it is in the body: if there is any virus, it is in the spirit. [[src:b1p150l23]]

Perrin doubles over. The cloth comes away dark. He stares at it and says nothing. Gwinne crosses to him at once and turns the boy's face to the light.

MADAME VAUX
Is the child sick?

GWINNE
Sick from this room. From the very thing you praise.

Senior wets a rag and lays it on Perrin's neck, then returns to his page. The Adept keeps his eye on the fire.

GWINNE
Spirits are as impure as bodies: and why not more so? [[src:b1p150l15]]

GWINNE
Some spirits harm by their breath; indeed, they even kill. [[src:b1p150l18]]

GWINNE
We have heard of spiritual poisons, and they are capital; compared to which material ones are little mortal. [[src:b1p150l19]]

GWINNE
In evils, even those are barely harmful, these are most harmful: the force is slower in those; but more violent in these. [[src:b1p150l22]]

THE ADEPT
Fire cleanses. It cannot make a poison of what is pure.

GWINNE
Fire does not delete this, but renders it worse, and nearly deleterious: as almost happens in others. [[src:b1p150l24]]

GWINNE
"Death is in the pot": which Nature hates. [[src:b1p150l6]]

The Adept sets down his tongs. For the first time he faces Gwinne fully.

THE ADEPT
You speak of what kills. I will speak of why bodies fail, and how far each one falls.

THE ADEPT
Through this, therefore, we find by truthful discovery a marvelous genus of two secrets. [[src:b3p195l1]]

THE ADEPT
The first is the triple cause of the corruption of each of the metals by fire. [[src:b3p195l2]]

THE ADEPT
The first of these causes is the inclusion of burning sulfurousness in the depth of their substance, which, through its inflammation, diminishes the whole substance of the bodies and destroys it into smoke by ultimate consumption, however much argentum vivum of good melting might exist in them. [[src:b3p195l3]]

THE ADEPT
The second cause is the multiplication of the exterior flame upon them, which penetrates them and resolves them with itself into smoke, regardless of their degree of fixation. [[src:b3p195l4]]

THE ADEPT
The third cause is the rarefaction of the bodies themselves through calcination. [[src:b3p195l5]]

GWINNE
And when all three meet?

THE ADEPT
If, therefore, all the causes of corruption coincide, it is necessary that the bodies be corrupted to the greatest degree. [[src:b3p195l7]]

THE ADEPT
If, therefore, all causes of the corruption of metals agree, it is necessary that bodies be corrupted most of all. [[src:b2p272l2]]

The Adept takes up four small ingots and sets them in a row on the bench.

THE ADEPT
Through this, therefore, you will be able to elicit a great secret: Since bodies with a greater quantity of argentum vivum are found to be of the greatest perfection; therefore, the more the quantity of argentum vivum in bodies that are diminished from perfection, the more they must necessarily approximate to perfection. [[src:b3p213l0]]

THE ADEPT
For which reason, therefore, from the things already said, it is evident that Jupiter most approximates to the perfect; since it participates in the perfection of argentum vivum more. [[src:b3p213l2]]

THE ADEPT
Saturn, in truth, less: Venus still less: Mars, in truth, least of all, as far as it depends upon the causes of perfection. [[src:b3p213l3]]

GWINNE
A ladder of defects, each rung measured. And because you can measure it you think you can mend it.

THE ADEPT
What is measured can be supplied.

Madame Vaux steps between them and taps her ledger against the bench.

MADAME VAUX
Gentlemen. I did not lend this house for a lecture. One thing only concerns me. Can the stone be made, or not?

GWINNE
There. Hear her. She asks the question you have all been careful to keep for last.

GWINNE
But whether it can be prepared (whether it can be compared by our own effort, or prepared by another's art) is a question called into controversy. [[src:b1p209l21]]

GWINNE
Controversy and question, as they differ: unless this one is through tortures. [[src:b1p209l22]]

GWINNE
The example does nothing, which resolves a suit with a suit. [[src:b1p209l23]]

GWINNE
Indeed, the question precedes, by which it is asked whether it exists, what it is, what it can do, how it can be prepared. [[src:b1p209l24]]

GWINNE
But here is a cart before the horse. [[src:b1p209l25]]

Madame Vaux looks from the physician to the fire, and closes her ledger. Perrin coughs again, softly, into the cloth.

# ACT 3 — Act III — The Fire and the Reckoning

ACT III — THE FIRE AND THE RECKONING

INT. LOCKED LABORATORY — NIGHT

The furnace throbs. Perrin sags between two stools, jaw slack, hands trembling. THE ADEPT steps back from the vessel, spent. SENIOR, old and steady, takes the tongs from him and settles before the fire. MADAME VAUX stands by the barred door, a ledger under her arm.

SENIOR
Sit. You have not slept.

The Adept helps Perrin to a bench. Senior addresses the vessel as if instructing a class.

SENIOR
And note that not everything should be put into the preparation at once, as the experts do—that is, one part should be tested so that no error occurs in the whole—or two in which your vessels may hang. [[src:b2p251l0]]

SENIOR
It is more tolerable to prolong under moderation than to sin irrecoverably under excess. [[src:b2p251l2]]

MADAME VAUX
How long does this go on?

SENIOR
Follow its nature according to the signs and keys handed down, and they will not permit you to err. [[src:b2p251l10]]

He adjusts the flame and begins to count on his fingers.

SENIOR
Let the humid and white stone, well-fermented, be taken, and let it be washed with one third of nine, and let it putrefy little by little and part by part, until it is whitened in 150 days—that is, 21 days of one name—and this is according to Senior. [[src:b2p251l13]]

MADAME VAUX
A hundred and fifty days.

SENIOR
He says that the first luminous work is to wash, to whiten, and to putrefy for 150 days, and this is the whitening of the whole and the flight of shadows from it. [[src:b2p251l14]]

SENIOR
And perhaps whiteness will appear in 70 days, that is, 10 weeks. [[src:b2p251l15]]

Madame Vaux opens her ledger and begins, silently, to reckon the fuel against the days.

SENIOR
Because as Rafis says in the Book of Lights: It never becomes black at the end, and if anything black proceeds, the medicine is imperfect. [[src:b2p199l1]]

SENIOR
And Senior says: If blackness remains in it after its rubification, you have sinned in its preparation, and you have corrupted whatever you have worked, and you will die from the pain of sin and poverty, because these are incomparable riches. [[src:b2p199l2]]

MADAME VAUX
So. Ten weeks at the least, and every week of it my coal, my candle, my roof.

She closes the ledger with a snap.

THE ADEPT
Sit with me, all of you. I will tell you where I have been.

The Adept crouches by Perrin, his voice low.

THE ADEPT
For this reason, some of the Philosophorum thought that the art could not be reached through this. [[src:b3p222l2]]

THE ADEPT
But we ourselves, in our own time, investigating this science, have arrived at the truth: that likewise, by no manner of preparation of our ingenuity, could we illuminate the bodies with the complement of their bright splendor without it happening that they were entirely corrupted, tainted, and rather, thoroughly blackened. [[src:b3p222l3]]

THE ADEPT
For which reason, we too were brought into a stupor, and for a long space of time, we hid under the shade of despair. [[src:b3p222l4]]

THE ADEPT
Returning, therefore, to our heart, tormenting ourselves with the afflictions of immense meditation of thoughts, we looked back from the perfection of the bodies the pores diminished, existing as foul in the depth of their nature: and nothing bright is found in them, since it is not in them according to nature. [[src:b3p222l5]]

SENIOR
But you did not stay under that shade.

THE ADEPT
No. I came back to the fire.

THE ADEPT
Therefore, the wise artifex should study our volumes, collecting our true intent which has been dispersed; which we have proposed in various places, lest it be published to the wicked or the ignorant. [[src:b3p322l0]]

THE ADEPT
He should test the collected [knowledge] until, by studying and experimenting with the persistence of an ingenious labor, he arrives at the complete cognition. [[src:b3p322l1]]

THE ADEPT
Therefore, the artifex should apply himself, and he will find it. [[src:b3p322l2]]

He grips Perrin's shoulder, then looks to Senior.

THE ADEPT
Therefore, sons of doctrine, search for this most excellent gift of God kept for you alone. [[src:b3p269l5]]

THE ADEPT
Foolish sons of wickedness and malevolent and immense depravity, flee from this science, since it is hostile and adverse to you, and it will set you in the misery of poverty. [[src:b3p269l6]]

A hiss from the vessel. GWINNE, who has watched from the shadow all night, comes forward with a rag and lifts the lid.

GWINNE
Let us see the gift of God, then.

He tilts the vessel to the candle and looks long.

GWINNE
But what if it strips off the metallic form of gold? [[src:b1p173l6]]

THE ADEPT
It strips nothing. It perfects.

GWINNE
It will spit out the beautiful gold, it will despoil it. [[src:b1p173l7]]

GWINNE
What if the form is incorruptible, inseparable, so that it remains gold? [[src:b1p173l8]]

GWINNE
What if it is not gold, if the form of gold is stripped away? [[src:b1p173l9]]

GWINNE
I was expecting a herald who would extol the fame of gold; I experience a robber who takes away the form of gold. [[src:b1p173l10]]

THE ADEPT
You name a robber where a maker stands.

GWINNE
But he induces a new, irreducible one. [[src:b1p173l11]]

THE ADEPT
New, yes. Irreducible, yes.

GWINNE
New and irreducible do not cohere. [[src:b1p173l13]]

GWINNE
Irreducible was induced before, and extracted, but it cannot be reduced so that it is the same as it was before. [[src:b1p173l14]]

GWINNE
It is neither the same new thing, nor was it induced and extracted before. [[src:b1p173l15]]

THE ADEPT
The body is changed at the root. You cannot lead it back.

GWINNE
But that takes away not the form and mixture, but the continuity: therefore it is still reducible. [[src:b1p134l3]]

GWINNE
The internal form does not perish. [[src:b1p134l7]]

Gwinne sets the vessel down and turns to the Adept, gentler now.

GWINNE
Hear me not as a judge but as a physician. You are ill of this.

GWINNE
Alas, he will be detected: the mask is stripped away. [[src:b1p182l0]]

GWINNE
If I advise what is to be done, let him confess at last, I would urge, let him confess: let him put down the ridiculous mask. [[src:b1p182l1]]

GWINNE
The one salvation for the defeated is to hope for no salvation. [[src:b1p182l2]]

THE ADEPT
And what do you take me to have shackled?

GWINNE
For he has entangled not only his feet but his head in these shackles: and he imprudently brings not only his fortunes into danger, but also his hunger and faith into crime. [[src:b1p182l4]]

GWINNE
There is an old song for a man who will not stay ashore.

GWINNE
Why then do I not sing to him that from Horace? [[src:b1p182l9]]

GWINNE
O ship, will new surges carry you back out to sea? [[src:b1p182l10]]

GWINNE
Unless you owe A mockery to the winds, beware. [[src:b1p182l13]]

GWINNE
Are the waves of the Chemists not waves, and indeed triple waves? [[src:b1p182l19]]

THE ADEPT
Say it out. I will not flinch from it.

GWINNE
But so be it, he says; So be it: let men roar with shouting, the ropes with creaking, The heavy wave with the incursion of waves, the ether with thunder. [[src:b1p182l20]]

GWINNE
Rare swimmers appear in the vast abyss. and so The art fails, and the spirits fall; and as many deaths are seen to rush and break in as there are waves coming. [[src:b1p182l21]]

THE ADEPT
Then I accept the storm. I have been under it before.

A grey line shows at the shutter. Perrin's breathing changes, rattles, stops. Senior goes to him, touches his throat, and closes the boy's eyes.

SENIOR
He is gone.

Madame Vaux unbars the door. Cold light floods in. She begins pointing at the vessels and the furnace irons.

MADAME VAUX
The glass. The stills. The scales. All of it, against what is owed. I keep the house; I keep these.

She directs unseen porters. The equipment is carried past the dead boy and out. Senior remains at the cold hearth, an old parchment in his hands, and reads.

SENIOR
EVIDENT AND MANIFEST PROOF OF THE CHEMICAL ART. [[src:b3p20l0]]

SENIOR
Some years ago at Padua, a wonderful argument for the Alchemical art was discovered. [[src:b3p20l2]]

SENIOR
Inside this urn, another smaller one was found; when it was opened, two flasks were discovered, elaborately crafted; one made of silver, the other of gold, filled with a very pure liquid, by which a lamp still burning is believed to have been preserved for very many centuries. [[src:b3p20l4]]

SENIOR
On the little urns, these verses were inscribed: > Go away from here, worst of thieves, > What do you want with your prying eyes? > Go away from here with your Mercury wearing a hat and carrying a caduceus; > The Greatest makes this gift sacred to the greatest Pluto. [[src:b3p20l5]]

GWINNE
And still you will not say it was nothing.

THE ADEPT
I will say what it is.

THE ADEPT
For we consider this science to treat of perfect and imperfect bodies. [[src:b3p322l4]]

THE ADEPT
It also gives full knowledge of perfecting and of the corruption of matter and form. [[src:b3p322l5]]

MADAME VAUX
And poverty took the rest.

THE ADEPT
Yet, these people, oppressed by the utmost poverty and the need for all expenses, are forced to postpone this most excellent masterwork. [[src:b3p30l2]]

THE ADEPT
It is now therefore evident from what has been said what the impeding factors are in this art that hold one back, lest anyone attain its end. [[src:b3p30l4]]

Gwinne gathers his coat. The Adept does not move from the stripped bench where Perrin lies.

THE ADEPT
It is open to studious, wise, and intelligent investigators, but concealed to the less intelligent. [[src:b2p92l5]]

Gwinne pauses at the open door, says nothing, and goes out into the morning. Senior folds the parchment. The furnace ticks as it cools.

FADE OUT.

spine.title: The Sealed Flask: A Chronicle of Gold in Seven Hands
spine.logline: A small golden flask of philosophical water, sealed and buried by its maker, passes through diggers, goldsmiths, assayers and widows across centuries until it is finally opened and dissected at a physicians' disputation, where the question of whether art can make an incorruptible metal is answered at the cost of everyone who asked it.

beats.summary: In a hot workshop, the Author dictates while Zenobia decants a bright liquid into a small golden flask, stopping her hand whenever she works too fast. The naming of what is in the vessel takes longer than the pouring.

Zenobia asks whether a pinch of a cheaper powder might be added to make the flask go further. The Author strikes the powder from her palm and makes her repeat the prohibition until she can say it in her sleep.

Geber comes through from the furnace-room with a scale and a broken ingot, and insists on establishing what a metal even is before anyone claims to have made one. He enumerates how fire ruins bodies; the Author concedes the point without conceding the work.
A creditor's clerk waits at the door with the argument of the whole world against the art. Geber answers him at the threshold; the Author does not look up from the wax he is warming.
The flask is nested in a second urn and lowered into a pit by lamplight. The Author cuts an inscription into the lid to keep thieves off, and gives Zenobia a warning to repeat over the filled earth.

Centuries on, Bartolo's spade rings on stone outside Padua. The Notary is fetched, the urns are opened before witnesses, and the finding is entered in the register while Bartolo argues about his share.

Master Orsino buys the flask for the weight of its shell and tests that shell on the cement and the ash-bed, reading the method aloud from a battered volume as his boy works the bellows. The metal survives everything he does to it, which decides him to sell rather than melt.

In a prince's assay-house, Hieronymus Feld promises to make the flask's virtue go a thousandfold further, and lays out to his patron which base bodies he will begin with and in what order. The patron grants him a year, a cellar, and a quota.

Three years later the cellar is stripped, the quota unmet, and Feld works by a single candle with his hands blackened. He reckons up what has kept him from the end of the work, and Anna finds him at dawn slumped over the cold furnace.

Anna sells the flask and her husband's manuscripts to a physician's agent, who leafs through the papers and gives his opinion of the man who wrote them. She takes the money and asks him to buy the papers too, so that no one else follows them.

Ned sets the flask on a cushion before a college disputation. Gwinne states the question that has been set down for the day and notes how the learned have already divided over it long before the vessel arrived.
The flask is unwrapped and the room leans forward. Gwinne lets them stare, then turns the glitter against them, and orders the vessel weighed and touched on the stone rather than admired.

A proponent of the medicine explains that the operation draws off the soul of gold and leaves the dross. Gwinne demands the two halves be laid on the table separately and pursues him through the consequences until the man stops answering.

The talk turns from the drink to the greater claim, the projection that would make gold itself. Gwinne takes the claim apart clause by clause, and a second speaker's attempt to save it by appealing to reduction is cut off.

The proponent is unmasked before the assembly and told what would be the honest course; Gwinne describes the sea he has put himself out on. The court disperses, and Ned, left alone to carry the flask back to the strongbox, is given the old encouragement by a lingering artisan and turns it over in his hands.
