# ACT 1 — The Sealing

TITLE: The Sealed Flask: A Chronicle of Gold in Seven Hands

= ACT ONE: THE SEALING

INT. THE AUTHOR'S WORKSHOP - DAY

Heat hangs in the room. A low furnace breathes. ZENOBIA holds a clay dipper over a small golden flask. THE AUTHOR OF THE TABULA sits at a slanted desk, dictating, one hand raised.

ZENOBIA
It runs bright today. Shall I pour?

THE AUTHOR
Slowly. Name it before you spill it.

THE AUTHOR
The three higher ones, however, are an image of divine spirituality, in which is carried water, which they call gold, and they name this divine water of the nature of all moisture, from vinegars, urines, and milks, fats, bloods, and sperms. [[src:b2p24l2]]

ZENOBIA
You have said its names before. There are too many.

THE AUTHOR
There are exactly enough. Hold your hand.

Her hand tips. He stops it with a look.

THE AUTHOR
Similarly, they name this water the vivifying Cloud, the lower world, and by all these things they understand the Aqua foliata, which is the gold of the Philosophers, which the master Hermes called the Egg, having many names. [[src:b2p24l5]]

ZENOBIA
The dipper is nearly dry, master.

THE AUTHOR
Then the last of it deserves the longest saying.

THE AUTHOR
And the water is their gold, because it is the mother of gold, because it generates gold, according to Senior: And those three earths are one nature of one sphere, and of one kind: and it is to be understood similarly regarding the three saltings, and salted things, that is, the imbibitions with three thirds of nine parts. [[src:b2p189l6]]

The flask is full. Zenobia sets the dipper down.

THE AUTHOR
Also Maria said of it: Take the body of the magnesia which has been whitened and made similar to leaves, because it is that which puts poverty to flight, since it has no other medicine after God. [[src:b2p101l2]]


INT. THE AUTHOR'S WORKSHOP - CONTINUOUS

Zenobia produces a small twist of paper holding grey powder. She weighs it in her palm, glancing at the flask.

ZENOBIA
A pinch of this. Cheaper by far. The flask would go twice as far, and the buyers none the wiser.

The Author rises and strikes the powder from her hand. It scatters on the floor.

THE AUTHOR
Indeed, all the sages said, Do not cause anything alien to enter upon it, for it corrupts it. [[src:b2p69l6]]

ZENOBIA
One grain only.

THE AUTHOR
But if it enters, it will destroy it, and this will never be concluded with our stones and our bodies. [[src:b2p69l7]]

He holds her wrist and makes her look at the flask.

THE AUTHOR
Say it back.

ZENOBIA
Do not therefore be deceived by the plurality of names, but hold it as certain that each one is what it is, to which nothing alien is added. [[src:b2p171l1]]

THE AUTHOR
Again. Until you could say it asleep.

ZENOBIA
Therefore, investigate its companion, that is, brass, and add nothing else to it, and let men multiply names; if they were not multiplied, children would mock our wisdom. [[src:b2p171l2]]


INT. THE AUTHOR'S WORKSHOP - LATER

GEBER enters from the furnace-room carrying a hand-scale and a broken ingot. He sets the ingot on the desk with a knock.

GEBER
Before you call this made, tell me what a metal is. Name your kinds.

THE AUTHOR
Name them yourself. You brought the scale.

GEBER
There are six of them, namely: Gold, Silver, Lead, Tin, Brass or Copper, and Iron. [[src:b3p86l6]]

GEBER
We say, therefore, that a metal is a fusible mineral body, extendable under the hammer in every dimension. [[src:b3p86l7]]

GEBER
A metal is, moreover, of dense substance and very strong composition. [[src:b3p86l8]]

He taps the broken ingot.

GEBER
And yet fire ruins them. I have watched it happen every way it can.

THE AUTHOR
Say the ways, then.

GEBER
The first is the triple cause of the corruption of each of the metals by fire. [[src:b3p195l2]]

GEBER
If, therefore, all the causes of corruption coincide, it is necessary that the bodies be corrupted to the greatest degree. [[src:b3p195l7]]

THE AUTHOR
All that is true of bodies. I do not deny it.

THE AUTHOR
If, therefore, all causes of the corruption of metals agree, it is necessary that bodies be corrupted most of all. [[src:b2p272l2]]

GEBER
And still you seal your flask.

THE AUTHOR
And still I seal it.


INT. THE AUTHOR'S WORKSHOP - THRESHOLD - CONTINUOUS

A CREDITOR'S CLERK stands in the doorway with a ledger, unwilling to step over the threshold. The Author has returned to his desk, warming a stick of wax over a small flame, not looking up.

THE CLERK
My master sends the argument of the whole world. Hear it.

GEBER
Speak it at the door. You'll come no further.

THE CLERK
Furthermore, others argue based on what we see through experience, for this science has reached the ears of the prudent for more than a thousand years, and if it were possible and true, it would have been discovered a thousand times over by now. [[src:b3p38l0]]

THE CLERK
Similarly, since the philosophers have not dared to hand it down in their volumes, nor can we find any manifest truth in them, it is sufficiently probable that this science does not exist. [[src:b3p38l1]]

THE CLERK
Likewise, many princes of this world, possessing infinite treasure and an abundance of philosophers, desire to find this art; yet they have not been able to reach the fruit of this most precious art, which is surely a sufficient argument that this art is frivolous and a mere fabrication. [[src:b3p38l2]]

Geber sets down the scale and answers him across the sill.

GEBER
Our answer, however, is this: because they do not know all that is knowable concerning this matter, therefore the work is not found therein. [[src:b3p65l1]]

GEBER
They therefore posit the flaw of the conclusion because of the insufficiency of their own work. [[src:b3p65l2]]

The clerk closes his ledger. The Author never lifts his eyes from the wax.


EXT. A WALLED GARDEN - NIGHT

Lamplight. A pit is open in the ground. The golden flask has been nested inside a second, plain urn. Zenobia lowers it on a cord. The Author kneels at the lid with a chisel, cutting letters into the clay.

ZENOBIA
What do you carve?

THE AUTHOR
A gift for thieves. So they leave it alone.

He reads what he has cut.

THE AUTHOR
On the little urns, these verses were inscribed: > Go away from here, worst of thieves, > What do you want with your prying eyes? > Go away from here with your Mercury wearing a hat and carrying a caduceus; > The Greatest makes this gift sacred to the greatest Pluto. [[src:b3p20l5]]

He steps back. Zenobia begins to fill the earth over the urn.

THE AUTHOR
When it is covered, say this over it, and mean both halves.

ZENOBIA
Therefore, sons of doctrine, search for this most excellent gift of God kept for you alone. [[src:b3p269l5]]

ZENOBIA
Foolish sons of wickedness and malevolent and immense depravity, flee from this science, since it is hostile and adverse to you, and it will set you in the misery of poverty. [[src:b3p269l6]]

She tamps the last of the earth flat. The lamp gutters.

# ACT 2 — Many Hands

ACT TWO

MANY HANDS

EXT. A FIELD OUTSIDE PADUA - MORNING

Centuries later. Frost on the furrows. BARTOLO drives his spade down and the spade rings.

BARTOLO
Stone. Under a foot of dirt, and it rang like a bell.

He digs. A stone urn comes up, black with earth. Letters cut into the lid. He turns it in the light and cannot read them.

BARTOLO
Words. Somebody's words. Fetch the notary, he reads.

THE NOTARY enters with two witnesses and a portable desk. He kneels, sets out ink, opens a register.

THE NOTARY
Stand back from it until the witnesses have looked.

BARTOLO
I found it. My field, my spade, my back.

THE NOTARY
The field is the chapter's. Your back is your own.

The Notary breaks the seal of the lid. He reads the cut letters slowly.

THE NOTARY
On the little urns, these verses were inscribed: > Go away from here, worst of thieves, > What do you want with your prying eyes? > Go away from here with your Mercury wearing a hat and carrying a caduceus; > The Greatest makes this gift sacred to the greatest Pluto. [[src:b3p20l5]]

BARTOLO
And what does that mean for my share?

THE NOTARY
It means a dead man did not want you here.

He lifts the lid. He begins to write, speaking as he writes.

THE NOTARY
EVIDENT AND MANIFEST PROOF OF THE CHEMICAL ART. [[src:b3p20l0]]

THE NOTARY
Taken from the Antiquities of Petrus Apianus. [[src:b3p20l1]]

THE NOTARY
Some years ago at Padua, a wonderful argument for the Alchemical art was discovered. [[src:b3p20l2]]

He draws out a smaller urn, opens it, and sets two flasks on the cloth. One white, one yellow. The witnesses lean in.

THE NOTARY
Inside this urn, another smaller one was found; when it was opened, two flasks were discovered, elaborately crafted; one made of silver, the other of gold, filled with a very pure liquid, by which a lamp still burning is believed to have been preserved for very many centuries. [[src:b3p20l4]]

BARTOLO
Then it was burning down there while my grandfather was born.

THE NOTARY
That is what is believed. What is recorded is the weight.

BARTOLO
Record the digger too. Bartolo, of this field.

The Notary writes. He wraps the gold flask in the cloth.

THE NOTARY
You are recorded. Go and wash.

INT. THE SHOP OF MASTER ORSINO, PADUA - DAY

A goldsmith's furnace. A BOY at the bellows. ORSINO weighs the gold flask on a small balance, the liquid still sealed inside it.

ORSINO
The shell weighs what it weighs. I pay for the shell. The water in it I count as nothing.

BARTOLO
The water is the whole marvel.

ORSINO
I cannot sell a marvel by the ounce.

He counts coin into Bartolo's hand. Bartolo goes. Orsino sets the flask down, opens a battered volume on the bench, and props it with a file. As he reads, GEBER speaks from the book; Orsino's hands move to the words.

GEBER
Similarly, likewise, the examination of this ash-bed can be prepared in an earthen crucible, and blown around it; and similarly upon its face, so that it may be blown around what is to be examined. [[src:b3p277l0]]

The boy blows. Orsino beds a filing of the flask in the ash.

GEBER
These things having been sufficiently narrated, let us pass to the examination by cement, with its causes and its manifest and known experiences. [[src:b3p277l1]]

ORSINO
Cement, then. Brick dust, salt, vinegar. Boy, keep it even.

GEBER
We have said, therefore, that certain bodies are burned more, and others less, by the mode of calcination through fire: as those which contain a greater quantity of combustible sulfur; and those which contain less, burn less. [[src:b3p277l4]]

GEBER
Since, therefore, the Sun is of a lesser quantity of sulfur among other bodies, it is for that reason the least burned among all mineral bodies through the inflammation of fire. [[src:b3p277l5]]

GEBER
The Moon, however, after the Sun, participates the least in the quantity of sulfur among all remaining bodies; yet more than the Sun. [[src:b3p277l6]]

ORSINO
So the least sulphur burns least. Sun first, moon after. That is the whole of the trade in two sentences.

The boy blows. Time passes. Orsino draws the filing out with tongs and quenches it. He holds it to the window, then to the shadow under the bench.

GEBER
That which has held that clear and clean substance is manifested through its resplendent and radiating gleam: revealing itself not only by day, but also by night, and it needs no other proof. [[src:b3p187l4]]

ORSINO
It is brighter out of the fire than it went in.

GEBER
That it possesses a fixed nature without burning sulfur is clear through every operation of it with fire. [[src:b3p187l5]]

GEBER
For it is neither diminished nor inflamed. [[src:b3p187l6]]

ORSINO
Neither diminished nor inflamed. Boy, put down the bellows.

BOY
Do we melt it, master?

ORSINO
I have burned it, salted it, buried it in ash, and taken nothing from it. A thing I cannot spoil is worth more whole than melted. It goes north.

He wraps the flask and locks it in the cupboard.

INT. THE ASSAY-HOUSE OF A NORTHERN PRINCE - NIGHT

A long room of furnaces, clean and cold. THE MARGRAVE stands with his secretary. HIERONYMUS FELD sets the gold flask on the table between them.

THE MARGRAVE
My goldsmith says it survives every trial. What of it? It is one small bottle.

FELD
One bottle of the virtue itself. Give me leave and I will make it go a thousandfold further, into base bodies, in order.

THE MARGRAVE
What order?

FELD
Tin first. It is nearest.

FELD
Therefore, among all imperfecta corpora, Jupiter exists as the most splendid, most lucid, and of greater perfection. [[src:b3p96l2]]

FELD
After it, however, Venus is chosen for a more perfect mutation, being of difficult handling, but of shorter labor than Jupiter. [[src:b3p96l5]]

FELD
Saturn, however, after Venus, possesses a perfection in transmutation diminished from hers: for it is of easy handling, but exists as the longest labor. [[src:b3p96l6]]

FELD
Mars, however, is found among other imperfect bodies to have the least perfection in transmutation, being of the most difficult handling of all and found to be of the longest labor. [[src:b3p96l7]]

THE MARGRAVE
You will leave iron to the smiths, then.

FELD
Iron last, and gladly. Each body has its own defect, and each defect its own remedy.

FELD
Otherwise, however, with a medicine that perfects, and supplies the defect, and attenuates to the depth of the body, and palliates and tempers their darkness and foulness, and brings forth splendor, it happens that imperfect bodies behave themselves. [[src:b3p213l4]]

FELD
From these, therefore, it has been discovered by the truthful investigation of labor that different medicines are found for different metals, along with their preparation. [[src:b3p213l6]]

FELD
Therefore, the medicine of the second order is that which completes the imperfect [body] joined by a single difference of perfection. [[src:b3p254l4]]

THE MARGRAVE
A single difference. Then tin is one step from gold, by your reckoning.

FELD
One step, well made.

THE MARGRAVE
You have a year. The cellar under the mint, coal, and two men. At the year's end you deliver me eight marks of fine gold, assayed by my own officer.

FELD
Eight.

THE MARGRAVE
Eight. Write it, and both of you sign.

The secretary writes. Feld signs. He picks up the flask and holds it against the candle.

INT. THE CELLAR UNDER THE MINT - NIGHT, THREE YEARS LATER

The furnaces are gone. Bare brick, one cold hearth, one candle. FELD sits among opened books, his hands black to the wrist. The flask stands beside him, still sealed, nearly full.

FELD
Eight marks. Three years. Nothing on the cupel but a stain.

He pulls a book toward him and reads aloud, marking each item on his fingers, as if the fault were in the world and not in him.

FELD
It is appropriate, therefore, now only to narrate the impediments supervening from the outside, from accidents by which this glorious work is hindered. [[src:b3p30l0]]

FELD
For we see some who are ingenious and astute, not ignorant of the works of nature, and who follow the principles in this work—insofar as it was possible—and in all its works where there is investigation and phantasia, in all things that are regulated by the actions of nature within the lunar circle. [[src:b3p30l1]]

FELD
Yet, these people, oppressed by the utmost poverty and the need for all expenses, are forced to postpone this most excellent masterwork. [[src:b3p30l2]]

FELD
There are others who are curious, held back by the vanities, cares, and spectacles of this world, from which this science of ours retreats. [[src:b3p30l3]]

He stops. He looks at his own hands.

FELD
Poverty and spectacles. Neither is my case. Mine is in the crucible.

He turns to his own manuscript and reads what he wrote there in a better year.

FELD
But we ourselves, in our own time, investigating this science, have arrived at the truth: that likewise, by no manner of preparation of our ingenuity, could we illuminate the bodies with the complement of their bright splendor without it happening that they were entirely corrupted, tainted, and rather, thoroughly blackened. [[src:b3p222l3]]

FELD
For which reason, we too were brought into a stupor, and for a long space of time, we hid under the shade of despair. [[src:b3p222l4]]

FELD
Returning, therefore, to our heart, tormenting ourselves with the afflictions of immense meditation of thoughts, we looked back from the perfection of the bodies the pores diminished, existing as foul in the depth of their nature: and nothing bright is found in them, since it is not in them according to nature. [[src:b3p222l5]]

He sets down the manuscript and takes up the small old book that came north with the flask.

FELD
And Senior says: If blackness remains in it after its rubification, you have sinned in its preparation, and you have corrupted whatever you have worked, and you will die from the pain of sin and poverty, because these are incomparable riches. [[src:b2p199l2]]

The candle gutters. He puts his head down on the cold furnace mouth.

Grey light. ANNA FELD comes down the steps with bread and a lamp.

ANNA
Hieronymus.

She sets down the lamp. She touches his shoulder, then his hand.

ANNA
Hieronymus.

She stands a long moment. Then she blows out the candle he no longer needs.

INT. THE FELD HOUSE, THE UPPER ROOM - DAY

Boxes roped shut. ANNA at the table with the gold flask before her, wrapped in linen. THE AGENT, a physician's man, turns over the loose leaves of a manuscript.

THE AGENT
The bottle my master has already agreed to. The papers I was not sent for.

ANNA
The papers are three years of him.

THE AGENT
So I see.

He reads a passage, then another, his finger moving.

THE AGENT
Then the author is brought in against the vain workers of this art, who have neither root nor preparation in the least, saying: Every preparation is good for that thing, except this hidden preparation of the Philosophorum: but they themselves composed the prohibition of it in their act, because they always prepare, and are never prosperous. [[src:b2p229l3]]

ANNA
He copied that out himself.

THE AGENT
Men commonly copy out their own sentence.

THE AGENT
And so that their error may be more confirmed, and that they do not despair of that which they seek, they cannot [attain it], but they hope to find it. [[src:b2p229l5]]

THE AGENT
And concerning the composition of false books, Senior says: For he composed his book, thinking that he understood that hidden mystical thing, and he himself neither knows nor understands one letter of those things which he composed in his book, removed from the books of the Philosophorum. [[src:b2p229l6]]

THE AGENT
And if it is asked of him, he answers from them through similarity, and if they are proven to him, he defends himself through cavils and vain similarities. [[src:b2p229l7]]

ANNA
You did not know him.

THE AGENT
I have known forty of him. It is one man in forty coats.

THE AGENT
Such a one who does this seeks boasting. [[src:b2p92l1]]

THE AGENT
For he composed his book thinking that he understood that occult mystical thing, and he himself does not know, nor does he understand one letter of those things which he composed in his book, and if anything is asked of him from them, he responds through falsehood. [[src:b2p92l2]]

THE AGENT
And if he is proven wrong, he defends himself through cavil and vain similitudes. [[src:b2p92l3]]

ANNA
He defended himself to the Margrave for two hours. Then he came home and did not speak until morning.

The Agent puts the leaves down and counts money onto the table. Anna takes it and does not count it again.

ANNA
That is the debt to the coal merchant and half of the rest.

THE AGENT
Then we are done.

ANNA
Buy the papers.

THE AGENT
They are worth nothing.

ANNA
Then they are cheap. Buy them and carry them out of this town with the bottle. Somebody will find them in this house and begin at the place where he left off, and I will have a second one of him at my table.

The Agent looks at her. He adds two coins.

THE AGENT
For the papers.

He ropes the manuscript in with the linen bundle and lifts them together.

ANNA
Where do they go?

THE AGENT
To London. To a physician who does not believe a word of them.

ANNA
Good.

She opens the door for him. He goes out with the flask and the papers under one arm.

# ACT 3 — The Assay at Oxford

ACT THREE

INT. THE DISPUTATION HALL, OXFORD COLLEGE - DAY

A long table. Benches crowded with gowned physicians. NED enters carrying a small bundle, sets a golden flask upon a velvet cushion at the table's head, and steps back.

NED
The vessel, as it was found. Untouched.

GWINNE rises. He does not look at the flask yet, but at the assembly.

GWINNE
I. Potable Gold, whether it exists. [[src:b1p22l1]]

GWINNE
I. On Potable, drinkable, and portable gold. [[src:b1p22l6]]

GWINNE
You have quarrelled over this before ever the thing was brought in.

GWINNE
Soldiers clash over this, and most believe that it remains uncertain where victory stands. [[src:b1p22l3]]

GWINNE
The Platonists do not agree, nor do the Peripatetic schools. [[src:b1p22l4]]

A murmur along the benches.

GWINNE
But they have passed sentence concerning raw gold. [[src:b1p44l9]]

GWINNE
Does he prefer this, or the elixir? [[src:b1p44l10]]

Ned loosens the cloth about the flask. The gold catches the window light. The room leans in as one body.

GWINNE
Behold a face shining from afar, behold the splendid beginnings that Pindar persuades. [[src:b1p22l9]]

GWINNE
Why does Euphormio sing the triumph of Gold? [[src:b1p22l11]]

GWINNE
The doors themselves rattle with gold. [[src:b1p22l12]]

GWINNE
Golden-mouthed, and a beautiful head, whether golden, or brazen, or wooden, or earthen, when gold speaks, who is not enticed to listen? [[src:b1p22l13]]

He lets them stare. Then his voice hardens.

GWINNE
Who, gaping, does not embrace it? [[src:b1p22l15]]

GWINNE
Although it is a head, yet it is not this --a body without a heart. [[src:b1p22l16]]

GWINNE
Let the Lydian stone test the gold: the gold will test the man. [[src:b1p22l17]]

GWINNE
A proverb among the French: It is gold, which is worth gold. [[src:b1p22l18]]

GWINNE
But I fear that in a golden scabbard a leaden sword may be enclosed. [[src:b1p22l19]]

GWINNE
But here is the doubt: is it golden, or gilded; is it a lion, or covered in a lion's skin; is it a mystes, or one carrying mysteries? [[src:b1p22l8]]

He gestures to Ned.

GWINNE
Do not adore it. Weigh it. Lay it on the stone.

Ned carries the flask to a set of scales and a dark touchstone at the table's side.

INT. THE DISPUTATION HALL - CONTINUOUS

The FIRST DISPUTANT stands, eager, a paper in his hand.

FIRST DISPUTANT
The operation is gentle, sir. It draws off only the soul of the gold, the living tincture, and leaves the gross body behind.

GWINNE
In the purest gold, what is impure? [[src:b1p150l3]]

FIRST DISPUTANT
The body is dross. We take what is precious and let the rest fall.

GWINNE
But he separates the soul from the body here. [[src:b1p150l5]]

GWINNE
"Death is in the pot": which Nature hates. [[src:b1p150l6]]

GWINNE
Lay me the two halves apart on this table. Body here. Soul there.

FIRST DISPUTANT
The soul cannot be laid down. It is drunk.

GWINNE
Let him send me the body of the gold; I remit the soul to him. [[src:b1p150l8]]

GWINNE
Is the body of gold impure? [[src:b1p150l9]]

FIRST DISPUTANT
Impure enough to be left behind, else why divide it?

GWINNE
But gold is extremely homogeneous to this; whose particles are of the same reason: so either both parts are pure, or it is impure. [[src:b1p150l12]]

The First Disputant opens his mouth, closes it.

GWINNE
If there is any virtue in gold, it is in the body: if there is any virus, it is in the spirit. [[src:b1p150l23]]

GWINNE
Fire does not delete this, but renders it worse, and nearly deleterious: as almost happens in others. [[src:b1p150l24]]

The First Disputant sits. He does not answer.

INT. THE DISPUTATION HALL - CONTINUOUS

GWINNE
Let us pass from the drink to the greater boast. The projection. The making of gold itself.

He holds up the flask.

GWINNE
But what if it strips off the metallic form of gold? [[src:b1p173l6]]

GWINNE
It will spit out the beautiful gold, it will despoil it. [[src:b1p173l7]]

GWINNE
What if the form is incorruptible, inseparable, so that it remains gold? [[src:b1p173l8]]

GWINNE
What if it is not gold, if the form of gold is stripped away? [[src:b1p173l9]]

GWINNE
I was expecting a herald who would extol the fame of gold; I experience a robber who takes away the form of gold. [[src:b1p173l10]]

GWINNE
But to induce new, intrinsic forms, and therefore faculties from forms, and therefore dispositions to faculties—not of art, not of the craftsman, but of Nature, the architectonic maker, the art of God which is held, is considered a divine work. [[src:b1p173l16]]

The SECOND DISPUTANT rises to rescue the argument.

SECOND DISPUTANT
But nothing is lost, sir. Whatever the fire divides may be brought back together.

SECOND DISPUTANT
But that takes away not the form and mixture, but the continuity: therefore it is still reducible. [[src:b1p134l3]]

SECOND DISPUTANT
The internal form does not perish. [[src:b1p134l7]]

GWINNE
Sophists philosophize for Cicero; but either for the sake of ostentation, or for gain: thus Chemists. [[src:b1p134l11]]

The Second Disputant sits, silenced.

INT. THE DISPUTATION HALL - LATER

Gwinne turns to face the whole assembly, the flask before him.

GWINNE
Alas, he will be detected: the mask is stripped away. [[src:b1p182l0]]

GWINNE
If I advise what is to be done, let him confess at last, I would urge, let him confess: let him put down the ridiculous mask. [[src:b1p182l1]]

GWINNE
For he has entangled not only his feet but his head in these shackles: and he imprudently brings not only his fortunes into danger, but also his hunger and faith into crime. [[src:b1p182l4]]

GWINNE
O ship, will new surges carry you back out to sea? [[src:b1p182l10]]

GWINNE
Rare swimmers appear in the vast abyss. and so The art fails, and the spirits fall; and as many deaths are seen to rush and break in as there are waves coming. [[src:b1p182l21]]

GWINNE
The one salvation for the defeated is to hope for no salvation. [[src:b1p182l2]]

He closes his book. The physicians rise, gather their gowns, and file out in low argument. The hall empties. NED comes forward to reclaim the flask for the strongbox. An ARTISAN, who has lingered by the door, watches him wrap it.

ARTISAN
To this question it must be said that the water is coagulated with the tincture, and I have seen [this] through experience. [[src:b2p311l2]]

NED
And if a man tried, and tried again?

ARTISAN
Therefore, the artifex should apply himself, and he will find it. [[src:b3p322l2]]

The artisan goes. Ned stands alone with the flask, turning it slowly over in his hands, watching the light run across the gold.

NED
Back to the dark, then.

He pockets it and blows out the candle.
